## The Problem

Below are some sentences in **Swahili** (a Bantu language spoken across East Africa) along with their English translations. Study the data carefully.

```{=html}
<table class="lang-data">
<thead>
<tr><th>#</th><th>Swahili</th><th>English</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>1</td><td>Ninapenda</td><td>I love</td></tr>
<tr><td>2</td><td>Unapenda</td><td>You (sg.) love</td></tr>
<tr><td>3</td><td>Anapenda</td><td>He/she loves</td></tr>
<tr><td>4</td><td>Ninapika</td><td>I cook</td></tr>
<tr><td>5</td><td>Unapika</td><td>You (sg.) cook</td></tr>
<tr><td>6</td><td>Anapika</td><td>He/she cooks</td></tr>
<tr><td>7</td><td>Nilipenda</td><td>I loved</td></tr>
<tr><td>8</td><td>Ulipenda</td><td>You (sg.) loved</td></tr>
<tr><td>9</td><td>Alipenda</td><td>He/she loved</td></tr>
<tr><td>10</td><td>Nitapenda</td><td>I will love</td></tr>
<tr><td>11</td><td>Utapenda</td><td>You (sg.) will love</td></tr>
<tr><td>12</td><td>Atapenda</td><td>He/she will love</td></tr>
<tr><td>13</td><td>Ninapendana</td><td>We love each other (I+another)</td></tr>
<tr><td>14</td><td>Wanapenda</td><td>They love</td></tr>
<tr><td>15</td><td>Walipika</td><td>They cooked</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```

### Questions

**A.** Identify and describe the morphemes (meaningful units) that make up Swahili verbs. What does each part contribute to meaning?

**B.** Translate the following into Swahili:

1. They will cook
2. He/she cooked  
3. You (sg.) will love

**C.** What is the Swahili word for "love" (the verb root)? For "cook"?

**D.** *(Challenge)* The word `Ninapendana` in row 13 contains an extra morpheme. What does `-ana` mean? Predict the Swahili for "They cook each other."

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Finding morpheme boundaries</summary>

Now compare rows 1, 7, and 10 — all three use "I" as subject, but with different tenses. Line up the words:

- `Ni-na-penda`
- `Ni-li-penda`  
- `Ni-ta-penda`

Do you see a pattern? Each word is built from **slots**: `SUBJECT + TENSE + ROOT`. Try identifying which syllable fills each slot.
</details>
:::

::: {.hint-block}
<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — The subject prefixes</summary>

| Person | Prefix |
|--------|--------|
| I | Ni- |
| You (sg.) | U- |
| He/She | A- |
| They | Wa- |

Now what are the tense markers?
</details>
:::

## Solution

::: {.solution-block}
### Solution Header {.solution-header}
Full worked solution
:::

### Step 1: Identify the verb root

Comparing sentences with the same subject and tense but different verbs:

- `Ninapenda` (I love) vs `Ninapika` (I cook)

The shared material is `Nina-`. The differing parts are **`penda`** (love) and **`pika`** (cook). These are the verb roots.

✅ **penda** = "love" &emsp; **pika** = "cook"

### Step 2: Segment the verbs

Each Swahili verb has the structure:

$$\text{SUBJECT PREFIX} + \text{TENSE MARKER} + \text{VERB ROOT}$$

| Example | Subject | Tense | Root |
|---------|---------|-------|------|
| Ni-na-penda | Ni (I) | na (present) | penda |
| U-na-penda  | U (you sg.) | na (present) | penda |
| A-na-penda  | A (he/she) | na (present) | penda |
| Ni-li-penda | Ni (I) | li (past) | penda |
| Ni-ta-penda | Ni (I) | ta (future) | penda |
| Wa-na-penda | Wa (they) | na (present) | penda |

### Step 3: The full paradigm

**Subject prefixes:**

| Person | Prefix |
|--------|--------|
| I | Ni- |
| You (sg.) | U- |
| He/She | A- |
| They | Wa- |

**Tense markers:**

| Tense | Marker |
|-------|--------|
| Present | -na- |
| Past | -li- |
| Future | -ta- |

### Step 4: Answers to Part B

1. "They will cook" → Wa + ta + pika = **Watapika** ✓
2. "He/she cooked" → A + li + pika = **Alipika** ✓
3. "You (sg.) will love" → U + ta + penda = **Utapenda** ✓

### Step 5: The reciprocal `-ana` (Challenge)

`Ninapendana` = Ni + na + penda + **ana** = "I love each other [with another]"

The suffix **`-ana`** marks **reciprocal action** — the participants do the action to each other.

"They cook each other" → Wa + na + pika + ana = **Wanapikaana**

### Linguistic Commentary

Swahili is a **Bantu language**, and this problem showcases its highly **agglutinative** morphology — words are built by gluing morphemes together with minimal phonological change at the boundaries. Unlike English (where "I love" vs "she loves" only adds an *-s*), Swahili encodes both subject agreement and tense as prefixes.

This slot-based morphology is very common in Bantu languages and is one reason they're frequently featured in linguistics olympiads — the patterns are rich but discoverable.

**Related concepts:** agglutination, morpheme segmentation, agreement morphology, verbal aspect
